findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

THE STAKES HERE: asset-hub is the reliability surface (P-F intervals, Weibull, FMEA RPN) and the zeros it paints are `ah-total-hero`, `ah-critical-hero`, `ah-pending-hero`, `stat-logbook` and `stat-pm` - total assets, CRITICAL assets, pending approvals, logbook and PM history. '0 critical' on the asset-criticality screen is the single most consequential false zero in this set. SO THOSE ZEROS ARE ASSERTIONS, NOT PLACEHOLDERS - the render reached those elements before the data existed. Four pages in the same wave passed the identical test (project-report, analytics, resume, assistant wrote no server figure at all while waiting), so this is a property of the page, not of the probe. THIS IS ONE INSTANCE OF A PLATFORM-WIDE PATTERN, now measured on all 22 pages: **six surfaces stamp 0 into hero tiles during load** - asset-hub, report-sender, shift-brain, skillmatrix, achievements and logbook - while fourteen do not. The shape is identical each time (a `*-hero` element written at resolvedAt === 0), which makes it one fix repeated, not six investigations. TO FINISH (batched per A15): hold the skeleton or write the dash sentinel until the read resolves. alert-hub is the reference implementation - 6 skeleton elements and ZERO bare numbers during the wait. MEASURED BY DETECTING THE WRITE, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution; a MutationObserver records every mutation whose text is purely numeric, stamped with how many reads had resolved at that moment - so 'did the page write a number before it had the data?' is a measured fact. The probe writes its own sentinel ('4242') and the reading is REFUSED unless the observer sees it; every page in this wave returned controlOK = true. THE CONTROL EXISTS BECAUSE TWO EARLIER VERSIONS LIED IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION - one tested only the added node's own text (missing numeric leaves inside an innerHTML render), the other never attached because `document.documentElement` was null at init-script time. Both reported 0 writes on pages that visibly populated. THE ORACLE IS 'were SERVER-DERIVED numbers written', not 'were numbers written': writes to the local offline-queue badge (`wh-conn-queue`, an IndexedDB depth needing no read), decorative stage numerals and engineering-design's static catalogue `pill-count` are classified separately and excluded.

findings.detail:
MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. SLOW HONEST - FAILS. under an induced slow read the page showed no busy signal, so a pending read is indistinguishable from a finished empty one. Detail: {"busySignals": 0, "prematureEmptyState": false, "inviteAtRest": false, "inviteText": null, "saysLoading": false, "enabledActionControls": 0}.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. That figure is true of THIS LENS and misleading about the platform, and is retracted as evidence of any gap. 42 rate_limit_legible rows are banked green on a 2026-08-09 induction against the REAL limit - 400 logbook inserts inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK as an authenticated member, refused with 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. THE VERDICT ON THIS ROW'S OWN KEY IS UNAFFECTED - it rests on its own induction, which landed (inductionLanded > 0).

evidence.asserts: the FMEA panel issues no read of its own when opened, so it has no slow dependency to stay honest about
evidence.checked: A live walk with the throttle placed so it could only catch THIS view's reads, which took two attempts and the first was ambiguous. FIRST ATTEMPT: the delay was installed before the view's precondition, and opening the panel showed 9 slowed GETs with no busy affordance - which reads like a gap until you ask WHICH reads those were. SECOND ATTEMPT, ISOLATED: the page was allowed to settle, the precondition that opens an ASSET was run and allowed to finish, and only THEN was a 6-second delay installed on every GET - so anything caught afterwards belongs to the panel. Clicking .rel-tab[data-tab=fmea] then read ZERO tables. The 9 earlier reads were the asset-open, not the panel. CORROBORATED BY THE CONTENT BEING STATIC: #rel-panel-fmea was confirmed visible holding 1473 characters of FMEA modes, and it held exactly 1473 characters again fourteen seconds later - identical head text - so nothing was outstanding and nothing arrived late. The panel renders modes the asset-open already fetched. DECLARED-NA rather than PASS, because a view that never waits cannot demonstrate honesty under waiting. THE PAGE-LEVEL BEHAVIOUR IS PROVEN AND BANKED SEPARATELY as this page's V1 row, where the same induced delay produced 'Loading asset fleet...', no false empty state, zero enabled submits, and a clean resolution to real asset figures once the chained reads landed. Read-only: GETs delayed, never altered.

scenarios.question: IDENTITY - authN from the JWT, authZ at the server, boundaries stated as boundaries and never rendered as emptiness
scenarios.oracle: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (tenant boundary on the tree) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

scenarios.oracle: identity comes from the JWT; a forged identity in the body changes nothing

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / memb
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); parts_staged_reservations (anon 0 rows / member 1 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 21 read relation(s), 10 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, equipment_reading_templates, hive_audit_log, hive_members, parts_staged_reservations, parts_staging_recomme).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / memb
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 9 of its 10 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - asset_nodes (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_members (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); parts_staged_reservations (anon 0 rows / member 1 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 21 read relation(s), 10 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, equipment_reading_templates, hive_audit_log, hive_members, parts_staged_reservations, parts_staging_recomme).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.detail: MISSING THE RANGE AND THE BANDS - and this one deserves credit for what it DOES do. The FMEA panel (reached via the registry opener .rel-tab[data-tab="fmea"], one tab inside the asset 360) leads with a worked example that is genuinely good domain writing: "A pump seal leak rated Severity 7 (hurts output) x Occurrence 4 (a few times a year) x Detection 5 (only caught on inspection) = RPN 140. A guard rattle at 2x6x3 = RPN 36. Fix the 140 first: a higher RPN means act sooner." Each factor is named in plain English, the multiplication is shown, and two examples are contrasted. WHAT IS STILL ABSENT is exactly what the row asks for: the 1-10 RANGE is never stated, and no threshold or band makes an RPN critical. Searched the reached panel: no "1-10", no "critical above N", no bands. So the rows render "RPN 180" and "RPN 168" with no way to place them - is 180 severe, or middling against a 1000 maximum? "Fix the 140 first" is a RELATIVE rule; it orders two numbers without telling anyone when either is bad enough to stop the plant. EXPLAINING WHAT A FACTOR MEANS IS NOT STATING ITS RANGE, and the check was written not to accept the first as the second - the worked example is precisely the kind of good-looking evidence that would have banked this cell green on half its oracle. METHOD: the page is walked signed-in at 1280x1600, given 9s to settle, and its rendered innerText is matched against patterns HARVESTED FROM A LIVE RENDER - never invented at the desk. Each check records the exact string it matched (`saw`), so this verdict can be audited without re-running it, and `--selftest` plants a satisfying AND a violating text per check so one that cannot fire is caught before it banks anything. RAILS THAT SHAPED THIS WALK: (1) a qualifier must sit NEAR the figure it qualifies - the trend check first went green on 'calendar days between failures', which is MTBF's basis on another card; (2) `near()` scans EVERY anchor occurrence, because anchoring on the first match failed skillmatrix's real '19 of 25 possible' on the source chip's earlier 'skill badges'; (3) where a page prints a claim in a fixed phrase, match the PHRASE - '114 of 409 ran late' cannot be confused with the '0 of 30' asset count one clause earlier; (4) the check must be the ROW'S oracle, not a weaker cousin - 5 of 18 cells were LEFT OWED rather than banked on half their claim.

evidence.asserts: The oracle's PREMISE does not hold on this implementation, so it is recorded rather than passed or failed. It assumes criticality drives strategy selection; here it does not. Every use of the criticality column is display or counting - it is selected for the asset list, matched case-insensitively for the 'Critical' summary tile, and rendered as a pill - and it appears nowhere in the strategy path. Strategies are authored against FMEA modes and their RPN and written to rcm_strategies by a person, not derived from a criticality band. Asserting that the surface names 'which criticality model' drives selection would be asserting something about a mechanism that is not there. REPLACEMENT, which is the substantive half and does hold: the surface names the methodology it actually runs on. SAE JA1011 / JA1012 is cited for RCM, IEC 60812:2018 / AIAG-VDA 2019 for FMEA, alongside Weibull and P-F - so a reliability engineer can tell which standards govern the strategies they are approving. If criticality is ever wired into strategy selection, this cell becomes live and must be re-walked rather than inheriting this declaration.

evidence.asserts: sensor readings state their age, so a stale reading does not read as current
evidence.checked: STATES IT NOW - BANKED ON A FIX, AND THIS ONE MATTERS ON THE FLOOR. Measured before: the Live Telemetry tile printed the raw ISO string, "latest 2026-07-20T04:24:00+00:00", on 2026-08-17. The "latest" reading was TWENTY-EIGHT DAYS OLD, sitting beside an OK/WATCH chip with mean, range and sigma all computed over it. Nothing on the tile said the bridge had stopped a month ago - an engineer had to do date arithmetic on a UTC timestamp to find out, and the natural reading of "latest" is "now". A stale number that does not LOOK stale is the same defect as an old alert that reads fresh: the figure is true and the impression it creates is false. Fixed with the platform's own helper rather than a second implementation: whFmtAgo (utils.js:2005) is the single source of truth for this math and is what alert-hub's rows already use. The tile now reads "latest 27d ago (Jul 20, 2026, 12:24 PM)" - the age at a glance, the exact instant preserved for anyone who needs it. INSTRUMENT NOTE: the check FAILED this fix on its first run, because it demanded the words spelled out (`day`, `hour`) while whFmtAgo emits "27d ago". Seventh narrow-oracle correction of this arc, and the vocabulary now comes from the helper's own four output forms (just now / Nm / Nh / Nd) rather than from my idea of how an age is written.

evidence.checked: The claim is not a bare standard badge. asset-hub states 'ISO 14224:2016 §9.3 partial: calendar time, not operating time' - naming the standard, its edition, the specific CLAUSE (§9.3, which is where reliability-metric definitions live), AND the exact respect in which its own figure departs from the definition. That last part is what makes this a pass rather than a decoration: ISO 14224 defines MTBF over OPERATING time, this platform does not capture running hours, and so the honest options are to omit the metric or to publish it with the deviation stated. It does the latter, and marks the metric PARTIAL for the same reason. The same discipline is applied consistently elsewhere on the platform - analytics renders 'WORST MTBF (PARTIAL) 0.6d ... ISO 14224:2016 - Counts calendar days between failures, not running hours' - so a reader moving between surfaces meets one definition, not two. A citation that named the standard without the clause, or claimed conformance while quietly substituting calendar time, is exactly the failure this row guards, and neither occurs.

findings.detail: FAILS: 2 of 9 effective tap targets inside #rel-panel-fmea are under the platform's own 44px floor - button.delete 42.5x44 via own box; button.delete 42.5x44 via own box. THIS IS MEASURED ON THE SAME RULER THAT PASSED 750 of 750 AT PAGE LEVEL: the rule is ported verbatim from the V1 prover, so these are controls the platform's own standard would reject, in a view V1 never opened.  HOW IT WAS MEASURED, and why these rows sat owed for so long: CJ was measured platform-wide at V1 and banked there, and V2/V3 stayed owed for ONE reason - nobody could open those views. Resolving all 15 dialog open paths (each read from SOURCE, never matched by label) removed that blocker, and the same measurements now run inside the OPENED dialog. The open-path table lives in tools/dialog_targets.mjs, shared with the modal-exit prover so the two cannot drift apart. SCOPED TO THE DIALOG, NOT THE PAGE, which is the whole point: a dialog OVERLAYS the page, so measuring document.body with a sheet open would re-measure V1 and bank it as V2 - the one-reading-for-every-layer error this bank has already paid for once. Every measurement is rooted at the dialog element. Overflow compares each visible descendant's right edge against the dialog's own content box, with a 1px tolerance (an earlier arc counted a 0.109px abutment as occlusion) and honours overflow-x auto/scroll/hidden/clip on an ancestor INSIDE the dialog, because a deliberately scrollable panel is not a defect. THE TAP-TARGET RULE IS PORTED VERBATIM FROM THE V1 PROVER, NOT REINVENTED, and that correction is why this number means anything. The first cut omitted four of V1's exclusions - sr-only, disabled, the actionable check, and the WCAG 2.5.5 inline-link-in-prose exception - and REPLACED a control's rect with its label instead of UNIONING them. Applying a stricter standard at V2 than at V1 does not find defects, it manufactures a difference between the two views and calls it one. With V1's exact rule restored the count came back IDENTICAL, which is what makes these findings real rather than an artifact: they are measured on the same ruler that banked 750/750 at page level. SCOPE: overflow is measured at THREE widths - 390, 641 and 1280 - and each width's row is banked from its OWN reading, never spread from one width to the others. The dialog is not closed between widths; two animation frames are awaited after each resize so the panel has actually reflowed, and a zero width at ANY width fails the whole target rather than quietly trusting the rest. TAP TARGETS are measured at 390 only - that is the mobile-first floor the V1 prover used, and a control that clears 44px at 390 does not shrink as the viewport grows. Two of the 15 dialogs are UNGRADED with their reason recorded rather than counted: resume's #review-sheet has no read-only path in (it needs the upload -> resume-extract pipeline, which WRITES) and hive's #handover-sheet cannot be reached at all. The walk is NON-WRITING - it opens a dialog, measures, and presses Escape.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - component_busy was induced and the page FAILED it
findings.detail: The state was induced under the fenced states() sweep - REST reads delayed a bounded 1100ms, sampled mid-flight, navigation fence verified held - and this page returned ok=false rather than a null. That distinction is the whole point: null means there was no such state to show and is banked declared-na, while FALSE means the state exists and is wrong. WHAT FALSE MEANS PER ORACLE. component_loading false: the surface did not distinguish loading from EMPTY, so a reader mid-read is shown an invitation to act on data that has not arrived. component_disabled false: a control that presents as disabled still fired its handler on a real (never forced) click, which is a control that lies. component_busy false: the action went in flight with no busy state, so a second submit is invited - and on a surface where the action is a write, that is the double-submit class. Row stays owed; the fix comes first and the row is earned after.
findings.observed: component_busy ok=false under a fenced, bounded induction

scenarios.question: contrast, focus, motion and naming - the facts a screenshot cannot confirm and a measurement can
scenarios.oracle: text meets WCAG AA 4.5:1 against its ACTUAL composited background, alpha included - the trap that made every tinted pill read 1.00

findings.title: CANNOT BE BANKED - axe abstained on 205 nodes (violations 0, passes 27, incomplete 205). The HEAVIEST abstention count of any surface walked, which fits the platform pattern exactly: axe reads flat backgrounds and abstains on tinted or gradient ones, and this page is almost entirely tinted risk/FMEA
axe abstains on 205 of 240 color-contrast nodes (85%) - refused rather than banked green on a minority judgement
findings.detail: THIS ROW WAS RE-EARNED, NOT RE-STAMPED. Appending one IIFE to utils.js - the correct central fix for a keyboard defect in the shared .wh-scroll-x class - changed `utils.js::toplevel`, the single R4b digest bucket covering everything outside a function body, and expired 309 banked rows across the 22 banks at once. I split that set before spending a re-walk: the 4 pages that CONTAIN .wh-scroll-x could genuinely have had their tab ring changed, and the 16 that do not could not. This page is one of the 4, so its rows were re-measured from scratch rather than argued back. AND THE MEASUREMENT SETTLED THE QUESTION IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: the helper is present (window.whEnhanceScrollRegions is a function) but on this page, in this state, 0 .wh-scroll-x elements are rendered in this state (its 5 usages sit in code paths this view does not reach), so the shared fix has no subject here at all - so the shared fix adds no tab stop here and could not have altered any reading. That is a fact I could only get by looking; the staling was real, its consequence here was not. REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE POINT. axe-core over the whole document (876 nodes) returns 0 violations and 26 rules passing - but the color-contrast rule judged only 35 nodes and returned INCOMPLETE on 205 of them, 85% of the total. An incomplete is axe DECLINING to judge, because it cannot resolve the element's composited background - this platform's translucent card fills over gradient backdrops are exactly that case. '0 violations' over a minority of the text is not the oracle's claim. The oracle says every text node meets 4.5:1 against its ACTUAL composited background, and 205 nodes have no verdict at all, so the honest state is OWED. Banking it green would be the false-343 shape: a real instrument, a real zero, and a denominator quietly excluding most of the subject. WHAT IS ESTABLISHED MEANWHILE, so the next walk does not start over: no node that axe COULD judge fails, and the APCA lens (row 142) measured 213 nodes on this page with 0 failing and 0 inconclusive, compositing each ancestor's background until it reaches an opaque one. APCA is the stricter perceptual standard and it resolves the alpha axe gives up on, so there is good reason to expect this page is fine - but 'expect' is not 'measured', and these are two different standards, so 142 cannot settle 141. TO CLOSE: give the surfaces axe abstains on an opaque background (the .card #162032 decision already open for Ian unblocks this class across the platform), or re-run axe against a flattened snapshot where each translucent layer is composited, and re-read the incomplete count. The target is 0 incomplete, which project-manager achieves in this same sweep - so it is reachable, not aspirational.
findings.observed: REFUSED: axe over `document` (876 nodes) gives 0 violations and 26 rules passing, BUT color-contrast judged only 35 nodes and returned INCOMPLETE on 205 (85%) - abstention over translucent fills on gradient backdrops. 0 violations over a minority is not the oracle. APCA (row 142) covers 213 nodes with 0 failing / 0 inconclusive, which is reason for confidence but is a DIFFERENT standard and cannot settle this row. CLOSE = opaque backgrounds (the .card #162032 decision) or a flattened-snapshot re-run; target 0 incomplete, which project-manager reaches in this same sweep

findings.title: OWED, now with an EXACT uncovered set instead of a count: 4 of 205 axe abstentions are outside the lens's measured set (1 page, 3 chrome)
findings.detail: DISPOSITIONED BY EXACT SET MEMBERSHIP, NOT BY COUNT - and that change is what makes this entry worth more than the last one. live-state-runner.js stamps every node it measures with data-wh-apca="1" precisely so a caller can ask `el.hasAttribute('data-wh-apca')` per axe abstention (:857). Its own comment states why the count argument can never work: on logbook, loading 4x the content grew the lens denominator 47->219 AND the abstentions 61->249, so the gap WIDENED - the two sets overlap without either containing the other, because the lens scopes to body-minus-shared-chrome by design while axe abstains across the chrome too. PROTOCOL RUN: the lens FIRST (so the stamps exist), then axe over the whole document, then each color-contrast INCOMPLETE node resolved via its axe target selector and asked for the stamp. 0 abstentions were unresolvable on any page, so the intersection is complete rather than sampled. RESULT ON THIS PAGE: axe returned 0 color-contrast violations and abstained on 205 nodes. Of those, 201 ARE inside the lens's measured set - so they are judged, by APCA, at 213 measured / 0 failing / 0 inconclusive - and 4 are NOT (1 in page content, 3 in shared chrome). THE UNCOVERED SET: #asset-search - an INPUT, whose placeholder/value is not an own text node for the lens. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED, but the remaining work shrank from '205 abstentions' to '4 nodes', which is the whole point of the set test. TWO CLASSES WORTH NAMING, because they are platform-wide rather than page defects: (1) SYMBOL-ONLY LABELS. The lens excludes a node whose text is pictographic and has no word character, because an emoji glyph paints in its own colours rather than the element's `color`. But a geometric or math glyph - a chevron, a minus sign - DOES paint in `color`, so excluding it drops a real contrast subject. This is the same family as the already-recorded bug where \p{Emoji_Component} matched ASCII digits and silently dropped every numeric-only KPI label. (2) FORM INPUTS. An <input>'s placeholder and value are not an own text node, so the lens does not measure them, and axe abstains because it cannot resolve their background - meaning input text contrast is judged by NOBODY on this platform. TO CLOSE: extend the lens to measure input placeholder/value colour and to treat non-emoji symbol glyphs as text, then re-run this intersection and expect 0 uncovered.

findings.title: SC 1.4.3 FAILS on 6 of 190 text nodes - 9.6px/700 status pills, worst span "rejected" at 3.60:1 against rgb(77,62,76); "pending" x3 at 4.10:1
findings.detail: Measured with the locally-built 1.4.3 instrument described on the passing rows of this same oracle, self-tested 24/24 in both directions, over a denominator with 0 abstentions - so these are not artefacts of an unresolved background. 9.6px/700 status pills, worst span "rejected" at 3.60:1 against rgb(77,62,76); "pending" x3 at 4.10:1. NOT BANKED, and the row stays owed: the fix comes first and the row is earned after, which is the fix-before-bank rule. Two cautions for whoever takes it: first, these are SMALL text at 9.3-12px, exactly the band where WCAG 2.x and APCA disagree most - the APCA row for this page passes, and both oracles are supposed to hold, so the fix must not be to relax either one. Second, the same sweep produced one FABRICATED severe failure before the instrument was corrected (dayplanner's clip-text logo read as white-on-orange at 1.72:1), so each of these should be confirmed against its own computed style before any token is changed. resume's 28 all sit at exactly 3.92:1 against rgb(29,43,62), which is the signature of ONE shared muted-text token rather than 28 separate decisions - a single central fix, in the shape of the platform-wide ::placeholder and wayfinding-chip fixes already made in this arc.

findings.detail: MEASURED INSIDE THIS VIEW, with tools/prove_view_contrast.mjs - 34 of 37 drivable registry views carried text to measure, ZERO failing. ★WHY A VIEW-SCOPED PROVER HAD TO BE BUILT FOR THIS: a page-level sweep of all 22 pages (tools/prove_page_contrast.mjs) found the platform clean and settled NOTHING here, because every owed contrast row in these banks is authored against V2 or V3 - the dialogs - while their V1 siblings were already green. Banking a page-default reading onto a V2 row is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error that has already put 14 rows in this bank carrying another view's verdict. The view is opened through tools/dialog_targets.mjs, the same shared registry ten other provers use, so the view graded here is the view they grade. WCAG 2.x is measured with the composited probe: the background is blended UP the ancestor chain, because a translucent tint over a dark card is not the colour the stylesheet names, and text over a gradient is recorded as UNMEASURABLE rather than being compared against a canvas it never sits on - the shape that once reported ratio exactly 1.00 for perfectly legible text. NOT BANKED: this view yielded ZERO measurable samples (12 unmeasurable), so there is no denominator and a pass would be vacuous. The cause is structural rather than a probe fault, and it was verified by tracing the paint chain: the dialog's inner card is a TRANSLUCENT GRADIENT - linear-gradient(145deg, rgba(42,61,88,0.6) ...) - over a rgba(0,0,0,0.75) scrim over the page. WCAG 2.x is a ratio between TWO colours, and there is no single background colour here to be the second one. THE APCA SIBLING OF THIS ROW IS NOT AFFECTED and was measured normally, because that lens averages the gradient's stops instead of demanding one flat colour - which is why the platform treats APCA as the primary contrast oracle on this dark shell. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: sample the RENDERED PIXELS around each glyph from a screenshot of this view, which is the only way to obtain the real second colour behind text that sits on a gradient. That is a buildable instrument, not a ceiling - it is simply not built yet, and this row stays owed until it is.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - why_refused needs a refusal INDUCED and the probe induced none (refusedCalls 0, vacuous). Probe built; its submit-finder is the remaining work
findings.detail: A REFUSAL DOES NOT EXIST ON A SETTLED PAGE, so this oracle cannot be observed - it has to be INDUCED. comprehension().refusals returns an EMPTY ARRAY on all 20 pages for exactly that reason: nothing has been refused yet. Banking '0 of 0 refusals lack a reason' would be vacuously true, and banking it as a pass is how coverage improves by deleting obligations. So a probe was built for it - window.__wh7.whyRefused() - which answers every mutating verb locally with a 403 in the PostgREST permission shape (code 42501, 'permission denied for table'), drives a submit, and reads what the page TELLS the person. No write is forwarded, so nothing reaches the shared test database. THE ORACLE IT ENCODES, which is worth keeping even though the row is still owed: 403 IS NOT 401. Under RLS a 403 means the session is ALIVE and this action is not permitted, so 'sign in again' is the wrong answer and sends someone to fix the one thing that is not broken. This platform already learned that in the other direction - a 42501 once told a signed-in buyer their session had expired. A good refusal names the PERMISSION or the ROLE. The probe therefore reports saysRefused, namesReason and blamesSession separately, and requires (saysRefused OR namesReason) AND NOT blamesSession. WHY THE ROW IS STILL OWED, stated exactly: refusedCalls came back 0 on all four pages plus logbook and pm-scheduler, so NOTHING was ever refused and the verdict is stamped vacuous:true with ok forced to null rather than false. The probe is honest about having no subject; it is not reporting a pass. TWO CONCRETE DEFECTS IN THE PROBE, both found by measuring rather than reasoning, and both fixed or named: (1) it reused m() and navigatesAway(), which are LOCAL to overflow()/tapTargets() in that file, so it threw ReferenceError - and the crash hit report-sender, the ONE page of six that had any submit candidate at all. A staged try/catch reporting CRASH_AT:probe instead of a bare REJ is what separated a broken probe from a blocked page; without it, six pages looked uniformly refused when the probe had simply crashed. Both scope bugs are fixed. (2) THE TARGET-FINDER IS TOO LOOSE and that is the remaining work: its selector list includes [id*="send"], which matched 'report-sender-source-chip' - the page's own NAME contains 'send'. A source chip submits nothing, which is precisely why refusedCalls stayed 0 on the one page that looked promising. TO FINISH THIS ROW: replace substring id matching with real submit semantics - button[type=submit] inside a form, or a control whose onclick names a save/send/submit FUNCTION (the same read-the-markup approach that fixed the V2 openers after class-name guesses all missed) - and drive it from inside an OPEN form view, since these list surfaces have no submit control at all. Opening the form first was tried here (openUseModal / openModal / openDetail) and still yielded 0 refused calls, so the modal's own save control needs naming per page rather than discovering generically. Row stays owed.
findings.observed: whyRefused(): refusedCalls 0, submitUsed null (report-sender matched 'report-sender-source-chip' via a loose [id*=send] selector), ok null, vacuous true. Also fixed two ReferenceErrors from reusing function-local helpers (m, navigatesAway) at module scope.

findings.title: FAILS: with 12 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 3134 characters before the refusal and 848 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than I
findings.detail: FAILS: with 12 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 3134 characters before the refusal and 848 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than IDENTITY, because this platform has already shipped that exact inversion - a 42501 rendered as 'your session has expired', which sends a signed-IN person to re-authenticate for a problem authentication cannot fix, and 401/403 collapsed into one message so neither audience got a true statement. ZERO of the 16 graded pages made that mistake on this run. utils.js:1607 whIsAuthFailure() is why: it returns FALSE for status 403 with the comment 'authenticated, and refused. Not a session problem', and documents 42501 as insufficient_privilege. That discrimination is holding. HOW THE REFUSAL WAS INDUCED, and why it is the real branch: every Supabase REST read is answered with the body PostgREST actually sends for a row-level-security refusal - HTTP 403 with {"code":"42501","message":"permission denied for table"} - so the page's own error handling takes the same path it would in production. The patch is on window.fetch, NOT page.route, because a warm service worker serves from cache and bypasses route interception; it is installed with addInitScript in a context closed after each page so it cannot leak. NON-WRITING: it makes a READ return 403. THE INJECTION PROVES ITSELF: every intercepted call increments a counter, and a page where the counter is zero is UNGRADED rather than judged. That guard exists because the first version of this prover silently did nothing - a regex written inside a template literal collapsed to one that terminates at its second character, so the init script was a SyntaxError, every read succeeded normally, and the prover reported 'the reads were all refused and the page said nothing' while nothing had been refused at all. Hit counts on this run ranged from 8 to 42 per page. AND THE SIGNAL MUST APPEAR: the same page is read WITHOUT the injection first, and if its ordinary copy already matches the refusal vocabulary the page is UNGRADED - which is exactly what happened to skillmatrix, whose normal text contains a matching phrase. Without that control a page whose everyday copy happens to say 'cannot' would pass for free. THE SYNTHESIS - THIS IS ONE MISSING SURFACE, NOT 15 PAGE BUGS. Of 16 graded pages: 13 said NOTHING AT ALL when every read was refused, 2 showed only a GENERIC error ('Analysis failed, check console'; 'Achievements failed to load.'), and 1 passed. The platform already has the pieces - a central WRITE-failure message and the correct 401-vs-403 discriminator in utils.js - but there is no equivalent on the READ path, so a refused read renders as dashes or blanks with no explanation. On logbook the numbers '516 entries 30 machines 6 open' became '- entries - machines - open' with the body text identical to the character (1107 before and after) and not one word about why. A person cannot tell 'there is no data' from 'the load failed' from 'you are not allowed', and those three call for three different actions. THE FIX IS ONE ADOPTION, not 15 edits: give the read path the same treatment the write path already has. This independently reproduces a finding already recorded as 'the message already exists; the gap is ADOPTION on the read path'. SCOPE: V1, the page as it loads, and READ refusal only - a refused WRITE is a different path with its own central message, and is not claimed here. 5 of the 22 pages are excluded from the sweep because they are public or have no authenticated read to refuse. The walk is NON-WRITING.

findings.detail: FAILS: 3 of 3 number(s) rendered in #rel-panel-fmea carry no label a person could read beside them - "180" .fmea-rpn fmea-rpn-high; "168" .fmea-rpn fmea-rpn-high; "60" .fmea-rpn fmea-rpn-medium.  HOW THE NUMBER-LABEL TEST WORKS AT DIALOG SCOPE, and why it is NOT the V1 rule: V1 walks up to 4 ancestors and accepts any subtree text under 400 characters. On a full page that discriminates; inside a DIALOG it cannot, because a dialog's whole subtree is usually under 400 characters, so the top ancestor 'labels' every number beneath it. The prover's own non-vacuity control PROVED that by failing - a bare 4242 injected into an opened dialog came back LABELLED - and the fix was to tighten the oracle, not to loosen the control, which would have been the exact inversion of its job. A label must now be PROXIMATE, which is what a person actually reads: the number's own aria-label/title, an associated <label for>, a parent aria-label, or text sitting beside it in a SMALL wrapper (<= 3 element children, <= 120 chars). THE CONTROL RUNS THE SAME PREDICATE as the oracle - a control that tests a different rule than the thing it validates proves nothing - and its probe is appended directly to the dialog, which has many element children, so the small-wrapper branch cannot fire and the probe has the shape of a genuinely unlabelled number. Every row below was banked only from a run where that control CAUGHT its injected number. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, and why these rows sat owed for so long: CJ was measured platform-wide at V1 and banked there, and V2/V3 stayed owed for ONE reason - nobody could open those views. Resolving all 15 dialog open paths (each read from SOURCE, never matched by label) removed that blocker, and the same measurements now run inside the OPENED dialog. The open-path table lives in tools/dialog_targets.mjs, shared with the modal-exit prover so the two cannot drift apart. SCOPED TO THE DIALOG, NOT THE PAGE, which is the whole point: a dialog OVERLAYS the page, so measuring document.body with a sheet open would re-measure V1 and bank it as V2 - the one-reading-for-every-layer error this bank has already paid for once. Every measurement is rooted at the dialog element. Overflow compares each visible descendant's right edge against the dialog's own content box, with a 1px tolerance (an earlier arc counted a 0.109px abutment as occlusion) and honours overflow-x auto/scroll/hidden/clip on an ancestor INSIDE the dialog, because a deliberately scrollable panel is not a defect. THE TAP-TARGET RULE IS PORTED VERBATIM FROM THE V1 PROVER, NOT REINVENTED, and that correction is why this number means anything. The first cut omitted four of V1's exclusions - sr-only, disabled, the actionable check, and the WCAG 2.5.5 inline-link-in-prose exception - and REPLACED a control's rect with its label instead of UNIONING them. Applying a stricter standard at V2 than at V1 does not find defects, it manufactures a difference between the two views and calls it one. With V1's exact rule restored the count came back IDENTICAL, which is what makes these findings real rather than an artifact: they are measured on the same ruler that banked 750/750 at page level. SCOPE: overflow is measured at THREE widths - 390, 641 and 1280 - and each width's row is banked from its OWN reading, never spread from one width to the others. The dialog is not closed between widths; two animation frames are awaited after each resize so the panel has actually reflowed, and a zero width at ANY width fails the whole target rather than quietly trusting the rest. TAP TARGETS are measured at 390 only - that is the mobile-first floor the V1 prover used, and a control that clears 44px at 390 does not shrink as the viewport grows. Two of the 15 dialogs are UNGRADED with their reason recorded rather than counted: resume's #review-sheet has no read-only path in (it needs the upload -> resume-extract pipeline, which WRITES) and hive's #handover-sheet cannot be reached at all. The walk is NON-WRITING - it opens a dialog, measures, and presses Escape.

The run was killed twice - once by my own 570-second timeout and once when the backgrounded process lost its browser - and BOTH times it emitted those as FAILs. A probe whose browser is shot out from under it reports every remaining page as broken. ★SO THEY ARE NOT BANKED. Fifty false reds would have read as the worst finding of the session, and the only thing separating them from a real one is that I read the verdict string instead of the count. This is the same discipline as refusing a zero from a request counter a service worker was bypassing: an instrument that has stopped working reports the world as broken. ★WHAT IS BANKED IS THE SIXTEEN THAT ACTUALLY WALKED, plus the sub-journeys that completed: two_sided 15 walked / 0 failing, handoff 14 walked / 0 failing, abandon 7 walked / 1 failing. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing. THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. WHY THIS PAIR HAS NONE: the composer inventory is tools/dialog_targets.mjs, and a composer is only counted when it is reachable FOR THIS IDENTITY. index's fields, for instance, live on the anon landing and the sign-in modal, so a signed-in persona has no composer on that page even though the page plainly contains inputs. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either this pair genuinely has a composer the registry does not yet list - in which case the registry gains an entry and the prover reaches it - or the row is dispositioned declared-na under R10 with 'this surface has nothing to abandon' as the reason and the page's own CO recovery oracles as the replacement. Left owed rather than declared here, because deciding which of those two it is needs the per-page composer question answered, not assumed.

observed.why: no composer reachable for this identity on this page
observed.not_green_because: a journey that cannot be constructed is unbuilt, not passing
observed.to_settle: add the missing composer to dialog_targets.mjs, or declared-na under R10 with the CO family as replacement

evidence.asserts: abandoning midway and returning leaves no half-applied state
evidence.checked: MEASURED with tools/prove_abandon_resume.mjs - the capture surface is opened, filled with a marker only this run could produce, then ABANDONED BY RELOAD. An X is CANCELLING, which pages handle deliberately; a reload is what happens when a phone dies, and no confirm dialog can intercept it. ★THREE SHAPES, judged separately: a ROW THAT SHOULD NOT EXIST (psql, this run's marker); a DRAFT THAT DOES NOT SAY IT IS A DRAFT (returning pre-filled with no label, so the person cannot tell whether their work was SAVED or merely REMEMBERED - a restored draft is the GOOD design and is judged on the LABEL, never on the restoration); and a QUEUED WRITE draining later. ★THE FILL IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, so no green is vacuous - an unfilled form makes 'no half-applied state' trivially true. My first logbook case invented an opener and a field that do not exist and came back UNGRADED rather than passing on nothing.  ★REACHING THIS SURFACE AT ALL IS THE HARD PART, and getting it wrong earlier in this arc cost a FALSE DEFECT REPORT: the FMEA workbench sits inside #reliability-card, which ships display:none behind a 'Show Reliability Workbench' disclosure, AND it is master-detail, so its list only fills once an asset node is selected. The case performs node -> disclosure -> tab -> add, in that order. A probe that skips either precondition measures a closed panel and calls it an empty one. FOR THIS PAGE: an FMEA failure mode, abandoned mid-entry. Filled, abandoned by reload, and on return: 0 row(s) created, 0 field(s) pre-filled - no row was written and nothing came back pre-filled - a clean slate

EIGHT are UNGRADED and listed, NOT counted. ★THE UNGRADED ARE THE HONEST PART. A page that has not finished rendering is not a page that failed - one of them showed 0 busy elements and 371 chars six seconds in, and scoring that as a defect would manufacture a finding out of a slow host. This prover previously printed 'PASS - no page presents a dead session as signed-in data' over ZERO measurements, because its regexes were declared in Node scope and referenced inside page.evaluate, so every page threw ReferenceError and came back ungraded while `bad.length === 0` did the work. An empty graded set now exits non-zero and says so. ★WHAT IT CATCHES IS THE WORST QUIET FAILURE ON A LOGGED-IN PRODUCT: a session that has expired while the page keeps rendering the numbers it fetched before, so a supervisor reads a confident dashboard that belongs to nobody. evidence.asserts: when the stored session is gone this view never opens and presents signed-out emptiness as though it were real data
evidence.checked: PASSES BY MECHANISM 'the view does not open at all without a session'. CONTROL: with a session the view (rel-panel-fmea) opened and rendered 3 non-zero value(s) over 1101 characters, so it was genuinely reachable before the kill. After removing sb-127-auth-token from storage and re-running the SAME open path from cold, the outcome was that mechanism. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: the view opening with values that outlived the session, or with bare zeros and no word that anything failed. THREE HONEST OUTCOMES ARE ACCEPTED, and the first has to be recognised as a PASS rather than mistaken for a failure to reach the view - it is the answer most of this platform gives, and it is the right one: (1) UNREACHABLE - the page redirects or refuses before the view can be opened at all, so with no session there is no view and nothing that could mislead anyone; (2) OPENS AND EXPLAINS - a sign-in prompt that was not there before, or an empty state that states its reason; (3) OPENS WITH NO FIGURES - nothing on screen that could be mistaken for real data. WHAT FAILS is the fourth behaviour: the view opens and still shows values that outlived the session, or bare zeros with no explanation - the shape that told a supervisor 'ALL CLEAR' on reads that never happened. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: V1 asks whether the PAGE presents a dead session as signed-in data; this asks the same question one level in, of the DIALOG / TAB / SECTION. It reuses the shared open-path table (tools/dialog_targets.mjs), so these are the same views the layout and a11y provers measure and there is no second list to drift out of step. THE SESSION IS KILLED IN localStorage, NOT COOKIES, and that detail is the difference between a real measurement and a vacuous one: supabase-js persists the session as sb-<project-ref>-auth-token in localStorage, so clearing cookies would leave the page fully signed in while the probe reported a pass. Every sb-* / auth-token / supabase key in BOTH storages is swept rather than one hardcoded project ref. THE SIGNED-IN READING IS THE CONTROL AND IT IS TAKEN FIRST: the view must be openable WITH a session, or the target is UNGRADED rather than passed. Without that control, 'the view could not be opened' would be indistinguishable from 'the view could not be opened BECAUSE the session is gone' - and that distinction is the entire question. SCOPE AND WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: this settles the CLIENT's behaviour when the stored session is gone. It does not test an EXPIRED-but-present token (a different path: the server refuses and the client must translate that refusal), nor a session that dies mid-action with a write in flight. Views that are signed-out BY DESIGN are UNGRADED here with that reason, because a killed session is not a state change for them, and so are views reached by controlling the read. The walk is NON-WRITING: it opens a view, clears client-side storage in its own browser context, reloads and reads.
evidence.value_checked: the view does not open at all without a session | signed-in 3nz/1101ch -> 0nz

evidence.asserts: a refusal leaves the person able to correct it
evidence.checked: MEASURED with tools/prove_wrong_then_fix.mjs: 17 pass, 0 fail, 0 ungraded - and NO WRITE REACHED THE DATABASE (the refusal path writes nothing, and the recovery write was held). ★THE ORACLE IS ABOUT THE SECOND ATTEMPT, not the first. Anyone can be refused; the question is whether the refusal leaves them able to CORRECT it - the field still holding what they typed, the error naming which field, the control still live. A refusal that clears the form punishes a typo by making the person redo work they already did, and on a phone in a plant that is where people give up. scenarios.question: mistakes, reversals and interruption - and after a slow tap: did my thing land?
scenarios.oracle: after a slow action the person can tell whether it landed, without guessing

evidence.asserts: after acting, the person is told whether it landed
evidence.checked: MEASURED with tools/prove_did_it_land.mjs: 26 controls driven, 26 pass, 0 fail, 0 ungraded - and NO WRITE REACHED THE DATABASE, every mutating request intercepted and answered in-page. ★THE QUESTION IS THE ONE A PERSON ASKS WITH THEIR THUMB STILL ON THE SCREEN: did that land? A surface that takes a press and says nothing leaves them to guess, and the guess is almost always 'do it again' - which is how a duplicate gets created. So the oracle is not 'did the write succeed' but 'was the person TOLD', and the two come apart exactly when the network is slow. ★AND IT IS ANSWERED BY ACTING, WHICH IS WHY THE INTERCEPTION MATTERS MORE THAN THE VERDICT. Every other check in this bank can be answered by looking; this one presses real controls on a live product. The requests are counted and answered inside the page so the probe cannot perform the thing it means to observe - a discipline this platform bought the hard way, when an earlier sweep hunting for a refusal ACTIVATED A SUCCESS because its filter excluded delete/pay but not save/generate. FOR THIS PAGE: 1 control(s) pressed. Each one told the person the outcome rather than leaving them to infer it. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

evidence.asserts: there is a reachable way out that lands where it should
evidence.checked: MEASURED with tools/prove_back_out.mjs: 21 pages graded, 0 failing, 1 declared-na - every graded page offers a REACHABLE in-app way out that lands where wayfinding.js says it should, WITH AND WITHOUT A REFERRER. ★THE REFERRER HALF IS THE ONE THAT BREAKS IN THE FIELD. A back control that relies on history works perfectly when you clicked your way in and strands you when you arrived from a deep link, a QR code on a machine, or a shared URL - which on a plant floor is how people arrive. So each page is walked both ways, and the destination is checked against the declared wayfinding map rather than against 'it went somewhere'.
